ceb.title: How the Bible Was Compiled
ceb.question: Who decided which books belong in the Bible? Didn't the Bible just fall from heaven complete?
ceb.answer: The Bible did not arrive as a single bound volume; it was assembled by the Catholic Church over centuries. In the early Church many writings circulated, and disputes arose over which were truly inspired (for example, some rejected Hebrews, James, Revelation, or 2 Peter). The canon was settled by Catholic councils under the Church's teaching authority: the regional councils of Rome (382), Hippo (393), and Carthage (397) listed the same 73 books Catholics use today. Christ never wrote a book but founded a Church (Mat 16:18) with authority to bind and loose (Mat 16:19), and that Church, guided by the Holy Spirit whom Jesus promised (Jn 16:13), discerned the canon. Thus one cannot appeal to 'the Bible alone' without first accepting the authority of the Church that identified those books. The table of contents is itself an act of Tradition.

en.answer_full:
> "I would not believe the Gospel, had not the authority of the Catholic Church already moved me."
> — St. Augustine of Hippo, *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus*, 5, 6 (c. 397 AD)

The canon of Scripture — the definitive list of books recognized as divinely inspired — is one of the most consequential and least examined assumptions in Christian life. Every Christian who picks up a Bible implicitly trusts that the 73 books (Catholic) or 66 books (Protestant) it contains are the right ones. But where does that trust come from? The Bible itself does not contain a table of contents, no book of Scripture claims to be the final member of a closed canon, and the early Church used a variety of collections for the first three centuries. The answer, historically and theologically, is that the Church defined the canon — and this fact has profound implications for the relationship between Scripture, Tradition, and ecclesial authority.

---

## The Historical Problem: No Self-Defining Canon

### The First Three Centuries

The New Testament as we know it did not exist as a bound collection during the apostolic era. Paul's letters circulated individually among churches; the Gospels were read in local communities. Alongside texts we now regard as canonical, other writings enjoyed widespread respect and liturgical use: the *Didache*, the *Shepherd of Hermas*, the *Epistle of Barnabas*, and 1 Clement were read as Scripture in various communities. The *Gospel of Thomas*, *Gospel of Peter*, and other Gnostic texts competed for authority in some regions.

This diversity was not chaotic indifference — it reflected the genuine difficulty of identifying which texts bore authentic apostolic authority. The question "which books are Scripture?" was not settled by simply reading the texts themselves; it required external criteria, communal discernment, and ultimately authoritative decision.

### The Councils That Settled the Canon

The canon was formally defined through a series of Church councils and papal pronouncements:

- **Synod of Rome (382 AD)** — Under Pope Damasus I, produced a list of canonical books matching the Catholic Bible, including all seven deuterocanonical books.
- **Council of Hippo (393 AD)** — Ratified the same list under the influence of St. Augustine.
- **Council of Carthage (397 and 419 AD)** — Reaffirmed and published the canon; requested Roman confirmation.
- **Council of Florence (1441 AD)** — Formally defined the canon for the universal Church.
- **Council of Trent (1546 AD)** — Solemnly defined the canon in response to the Protestant Reformation's removal of the deuterocanonical books.

St. Athanasius's 39th Festal Letter (367 AD) lists 27 New Testament books matching our canon — but it is a pastoral letter from a bishop, not a binding ecclesial definition. And Athanasius himself acknowledged the authority of the Church's discernment.

---

## Positive Biblical Evidence

### The Church as Pillar of Truth

*"The church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth"* (1 Timothy 3:15, NABRE). Paul identifies the Church — not Scripture — as the ground and bulwark of divine truth. This does not diminish Scripture; it locates Scripture within the living community that preserves and transmits it.

### The Spirit Guides Into All Truth

*"When he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you to all truth"* (John 16:13, NABRE). Jesus promises the Spirit's guidance to the apostolic community — the Church — not to individual readers of texts. The Spirit's guidance to "all truth" includes the truth of which texts bear divine inspiration.

### Oral Tradition Preceded Written Scripture

*"Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught, either by an oral statement or by a letter of ours"* (2 Thessalonians 2:15, NABRE). Paul explicitly places oral tradition alongside written letters as equally authoritative. The Word of God existed in oral form for decades before the New Testament was written, and for centuries before it was collected into a fixed canon.

---

## The Core Theological Distinction: Inspiration vs. Canonicity

The critical distinction is between **inspiration** and **canonicity**:

| Term | Definition | Who Determines It |
|------|-----------|-------------------|
| **Inspiration** | The divine quality by which God moved human authors to write without error in what they affirm for salvation | God alone — intrinsic to the text |
| **Canonicity** | The Church's recognition and declaration that a text possesses inspired status | The Church — through authoritative discernment guided by the Spirit |

A book does not become inspired because the Church declared it; rather, the Church identified which books were already inspired. But without the Church's authoritative recognition, no individual reader has a principled basis for trusting any particular collection as "the Bible." The Church's authority is logically prior to the canon as a collection.

---

## Church Fathers

> "I would not believe the Gospel, had not the authority of the Catholic Church already moved me."
> — St. Augustine of Hippo, *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus*, 5, 6 (c. 397 AD)

Augustine's famous statement is not a concession to ecclesial authoritarianism — it is a logical observation. The Gospel's authority reaches us through the Church's testimony. To accept the Gospel while rejecting the Church that preserved and canonized it is to undermine the very foundation of one's faith in Scripture.

> "The whole canon of Scripture is comprised in these books... Tobias, Judith, and the two books of Maccabees."
> — St. Augustine of Hippo, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, Ch. 8 (c. 397 AD)

Augustine explicitly includes the deuterocanonical books in his canon — the same books the Protestant Reformation removed in the sixteenth century.

> "We are not to suppose that the Holy Scriptures are incomplete. If any other text is not in the canon, then it is not canonical."
> — St. Athanasius of Alexandria, *Festal Letter 39* (367 AD)

Athanasius, the great defender of Nicene orthodoxy, understood canon as a closed and authoritative list — determined by the Church's discernment, not by individual readers.

---

## Ecumenical Council: Council of Trent (1546 AD)

The Council of Trent, responding to the Protestant Reformers' removal of seven Old Testament books, solemnly defined the canon:

> *"If anyone does not accept as sacred and canonical the aforesaid books in their entirety and with all their parts... and if both knowingly and deliberately he condemns the aforesaid tradition: let him be anathema."*

This definition reaffirmed the canon established at Hippo and Carthage over a millennium earlier — including Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Sirach, Wisdom, and Baruch.

---

## CCC References

| Reference | Teaching |
|-----------|----------|
| CCC 105 | God is the author of Sacred Scripture — he inspired human authors who wrote what he willed |
| CCC 107 | The inspired books teach truth without error for the sake of our salvation |
| CCC 120 | The apostolic Tradition enabled the Church to discern which writings belong to the list of sacred books |
| CCC 138 | The Church, to whom the transmission and interpretation of Revelation is entrusted, does not derive certainty from Scripture alone |

---

## Common Objections

**"The early Christians knew which books were Scripture — it was obvious."**

If it were obvious, there would have been no disputes. In fact, debates over the canonicity of Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, and Revelation continued for centuries in the East. The deuterocanonical books were read as Scripture by Greek-speaking Jews and the early Church for hundreds of years before Luther removed them. The "obviousness" of the canon is a retrospective illusion created by the very Church councils that settled the question.

**"The Reformers simply restored the original Hebrew canon."**

The canon Luther appealed to — the Palestinian Jewish canon — was itself not definitively settled until the Council of Jamnia (c. 90 AD), *after* Christianity began. The early Christians, including the apostles, used the Septuagint (LXX) — the Greek Old Testament that included the deuterocanonical books. Jesus and the New Testament authors quote the LXX far more than the Hebrew text. The "original Hebrew canon" argument relies on a post-Christian Jewish decision made in reaction to Christianity.

**"The Holy Spirit guides individual readers to recognize inspired books."**

If the Spirit guides individuals to recognize inspiration, why did Luther question James and Revelation? Why do different Protestant communities use different canons? The subjective witness of the Spirit cannot adjudicate between competing claims about canonicity — this is precisely why an authoritative communal voice is necessary. The Spirit guides the Church as a whole, not isolated readers.

---

The canon of Scripture is the Church's gift to Christians. She received the apostolic writings, preserved them through persecution, copied them by hand across centuries, discerned their inspired character, and formally defined their boundaries. To use the Bible while denying the authority of the Church that gave it to us is not only historically incoherent — it is a form of ingratitude that undermines the very foundation of one's access to God's written Word.
